News / Crypto Briefing / Russia opens regulated Bitcoin, Ether and USDT access to retail investors

Russia opens regulated Bitcoin, Ether and USDT access to retail investors 2 min read

BTCUSD ETHUSD USDTUSD Russia's central bank has authorized regulated retail access to Bitcoin, Ether and Tether's USDT for non-qualified investors, effective November 17, 2026. The rollout splits the investing public into two groups. Qualified investors, the category reserved for more experienced or better-capitalized participants, face no purchase limits and get broader access to crypto trading. Non-qualified investors, meaning most everyday retail buyers, are capped. They can purchase up to 300,000 rubles, approximately $3,600 to $3,700, per year through each licensed intermediary. Everyone has to clear two hurdles before placing a trade. Knowledge tests and risk disclosures are mandatory for all investors, qualified or not. Access also runs through a single type of channel. Transactions can only be conducted via licensed intermediaries such as brokers or registered exchange offices. The launch is staggered across venues. Other exchanges are slated to begin on November 22, while the Moscow Exchange is aiming for a pilot launch of trading by December 1, 2026. The authorization flows from Federal Law No. 282-FZ, which President Vladimir Putin signed on August 4, 2026. That law was designed to formalize the role of digital currencies and digital rights within the Russian economy. One line, however, remains firmly drawn. Paying for goods and services with crypto is still prohibited inside Russia. The research behind this rollout points to an expectation that trading volumes and retail participation could rise as a result. At 300,000 rubles per year per intermediary, individual retail flows are small. The inclusion of USDT stands out. A dollar-pegged stablecoin sitting alongside Bitcoin and Ether on an approved list gives Russian retail investors a regulated way to hold a dollar-linked digital asset. The per-intermediary wording of the cap is a detail worth tracking. How the limit applies in practice when investors use more than one licensed broker will shape how restrictive the rules really feel. Then there is the December 1 target for the Moscow Exchange pilot. Hitting that date would signal the infrastructure is ready, while a delay would suggest the plumbing needs more work. Finally, the payment prohibition caps how far this experiment can go. Trading is gaining legitimacy, but crypto's practical utility in the Russian economy stays boxed in until that rule changes, and nothing in the current framework suggests it will.

News / Crypto Briefing / Bitcoin falls below $70,000 as sell-off raises buying questions

Bitcoin falls below $70,000 as sell-off raises buying questions 1 min read

BTCUSD Bitcoin has slipped below $70,000. For an asset that set a record of $124,773 in October 2025, that is quite a comedown. The world's largest crypto has since lost more than half its value. Investors cut exposure to volatile, speculative assets as economic and political uncertainty climbed. The break below $70,000 was not a one-day event. Bitcoin first dipped to roughly $67,600, then kept sliding. Over a weekend of heavy selling, it reached a low near $62,000. It then clawed back part of the loss and traded between $64,000 and $65,000. At those levels, Bitcoin's market capitalization sits around $1.29 trillion. The asset has now logged six straight weekly declines. ETF money headed for the exits. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw outflows above $1 billion during a single week of the sell-off. BlackRock's IBIT, the biggest name in the category, was a notable source of the withdrawals. Leverage made it worse. Liquidations of leveraged positions topped $1.9 billion in a 24-hour window around the recent lows. Most of the damage hit traders betting on higher prices. Tech jitters spilled over. Risk appetite across markets weakened, with selling pressure tied to Nvidia among the visible stress points. Bitcoin has increasingly traded like a high-beta tech asset. Three signals stand out. First, ETF flows. Spot ETFs have become a key channel for institutional demand. A sustained return to inflows would suggest big allocators are stepping back in. Continued outflows would suggest the opposite. Second, the support zone. The range between $60,000 and $62,000 is the area now in focus for traders. Bitcoin already touched the top of that band during the weekend low and bounced. Third, the broader risk mood. Bitcoin's recent moves have tracked tech-stock sentiment and macro uncertainty closely. Economic data and the performance of names like Nvidia may say as much about Bitcoin's next move as anything happening on-chain. The $1.9 billion in liquidations is a reminder of how leverage turns a bad week into a terrible one.

News / Cointelegraph / Solana Foundation takes majority interest in crypto data firm CoinGecko

Solana Foundation takes majority interest in crypto data firm CoinGecko Less than 1 min read

SOLUSD Solana Foundation now holds a majority interest in crypto data aggregator CoinGecko, the foundation’s chief product officer, Vibhu Norby, said Tuesday. CoinGecko announced the backing but did not disclose the financial terms. It said it plans to use it to strengthen its data infrastructure, expand data coverage across tokenized real-world assets and derivatives, and develop onchain trading and market intelligence tools. The Solana Foundation “now has a majority interest in CoinGecko” and plans to collaborate on developing “new on-platform trading & DeFi experiences with Solana,” Norby said in a Tuesday X post. CoinGecko said its data methodologies would remain transparent and publicly accessible and that it would continue serving the broader crypto ecosystem. Its website, app and application programming interface, which supplies data to other services, will continue operating as usual. Founded in 2014, CoinGecko serves an average of over 10 million monthly users and receives over 200 million monthly page views, according to its About page. Cointelegraph has contacted the Solana Foundation and CoinGecko to ask about the size of the deal, but had not received a response by publication time.
